claims.text: The initial catalyst consists of Pt nanoparticles uniformly dispersed on graphene.
Thermal annealing at 300–500 °C in an inert atmosphere can induce strain and defect sites in Pt/graphene.
Plasma treatment can induce a controlled density of strain and defect sites in Pt/graphene.
The treatments alter surface lattice parameters and create defect sites at Pt nanoparticles and the Pt–graphene interface.
Strain and defects at the Pt–graphene interface shift the Pt d-band center.
A shift in the Pt d-band center changes the adsorption strength of reaction intermediates.
The proposed electronic modification optimizes adsorption energetics specifically for ethanol and its oxidation intermediates.
The modified electronic structure lowers activation barriers for critical proton–electron transfer steps.
Lower barriers and optimized adsorption improve ethanol-oxidation kinetics.
Optimally strained or defect-rich catalysts will have higher turnover frequencies and current densities than untreated Pt/graphene.
Optimally strained or defect-rich catalysts will favor complete 12-electron ethanol oxidation.
Controlled strain and interfacial defects enhance the catalyst's long-term durability.
Excessive thermal or plasma treatment causes Pt nanoparticle sintering.
Sintering caused by over-treatment degrades catalytic performance.
The proposed mechanism applies under moderate strain but not under conditions causing excessive sintering or irreversible morphological change.
A lack of statistically significant kinetic and selectivity improvement under moderate strain would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: Performance degradation after excessive treatment is called a clear falsification indicator, but excessive sintering is also declared outside the hypothesis's validity. Moreover, the formal falsification rule focuses on failure under moderate strain or an apparent improvement attributable to sintering, not degradation under excluded over-treatment conditions.
